summary: Commander is a command-line argument parser in six files. lib holds the whole library: Command, Option, Argument, Help, errors and did-you-mean suggestions. Everything else is verification and explanation, with 133 test files, 45 runnable examples, long-form docs including a Chinese translation, and hand-written TypeScript typings that are themselves type-tested.

districts.name: The Foundry
districts.purpose: The entire library: the command tree, options, arguments, help rendering, error types and similar-name suggestions.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: One test file per behaviour, named after the feature it pins, plus fixture programs for subcommand execution.

districts.name: The Showrooms
districts.purpose: Forty-five small runnable programs, one per feature, that double as the fastest way to learn the API.

districts.name: Knowledge District
districts.purpose: Long-form explanations that outgrew the readme: parsing and hooks, options and help in depth, terminology, deprecations and the release policy.

districts.name: The Drafting Office
districts.purpose: Hand-written TypeScript declarations with their own type tests, kept beside a JavaScript implementation.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: Two workflows: the test matrix and CodeQL analysis.

importantModules.role: The Command class: subcommands, parsing, action handlers, hooks and the program lifecycle. Almost the whole library.
Option definitions: flags, negation, variadic values, defaults, presets, choices and environment variable sources.
Positional argument definitions, including required, optional and variadic forms.
Help text generation: layout, wrapping, sorting and the hooks that let a program override any of it.
CommanderError and InvalidArgumentError, the typed failures a program can catch instead of exiting.
The did-you-mean suggestion shown after an unknown option or command.
The package entry point: re-exports the library and the default program instance.
The TypeScript surface, maintained by hand against the JavaScript implementation.

strengths: The library is six small files with one clear responsibility each, which is rare for a parser used this widely.
Tests are named after behaviour (options.variadic, options.required, useColor), so the suite reads as a specification.
Every feature has a runnable example, which makes the documentation checkable rather than merely written.
The hand-written typings carry their own type tests, so the TypeScript surface cannot drift silently.
A published release policy and a deprecations document set expectations for breaking changes.
concerns: lib/command.js carries most of the library, so nearly every change lands in the same file.
The typings are maintained separately from the JavaScript, which is a manual synchronisation step on every API change.
Documentation exists in three places at once: the readme, docs and the examples directory, with the Chinese translation to keep in step as well.
